verse_english: Dhp 75: For the means to profit and the path to quenching are two quite different things. A mendicant disciple of the Buddha, understanding what this really means, would never delight in honors, but rather would foster seclusion.

question: Which stories tell of a chief disciple leaving a rains retreat and asking for the requisites to be sent on?
title: The Story about the Elder Mahā Moggallāna
synopsis: After Elder Moggallāna had spent the Rains Retreat with five hundred bhikkhus the lay people still hadn’t donated the requisites; as he was leaving he asked for the requisites to be sent on, or that he be told; the bhikkhus reported it to the Buddha who explained it was concern for the donors and the young bhikkhus that made him ask so, and not craving, and then spoke a verse about the one without craving.
verse_english: Dhp 411: They have no clinging, knowledge has freed them of indecision, they’ve arrived at the objective, freedom from death: that’s who I declare a brahmin.

question: Which stories tell of a chief disciple leaving a rains retreat and asking for the requisites to be sent on?
title: The Story about Garahadinna
synopsis: Sirigutta supported the Buddha, but his friend Garahadinna supported the Nigaṇṭhas; Sirigutta proved that the Nigaṇṭhas do not know the past, present and future as they declared; and the Buddha proved his knowledge and power to Garahadinna, who became his disciple; then the Buddha spoke some verses. Lives, Bodhisatta
verse_english: Dhp 58: From a heap of trash discarded on the highway, a lotus might blossom, fragrant and delightful. / Dhp 59: So too, among those thought of as trash, a disciple of the perfect Buddha outshines with their wisdom the blind ordinary folk.

question: Which stories have Sāriputta asking the Buddha to show his relatives or friends the way to the Brahma world?
title: The Story about the Elder Sāriputta’s Brahmin Uncle
synopsis: Elder Sāriputta asked the Buddha to teach his uncle, who supported the Nigaṇṭhas, the true way to the Brahma world; and the Buddha spoke a verse with which he taught them.
verse_english: Dhp 106: Rather than a thousandfold sacrifice, every month for a full century, it’s better to honor for a single hour one who has developed themselves. That offering is better than the hundred year sacrifice.

question: Which stories have Sāriputta asking the Buddha to show his relatives or friends the way to the Brahma world?
title: The Story about the Elder Sāriputta’s Brahmin Companion
synopsis: Elder Sāriputta asked the Buddha to teach his friend, who offered animals in sacrifice, the true way to the Brahma world, and the Buddha gave him a teaching in a verse.
verse_english: Dhp 108: Whatever sacrifice or offering in the world a seeker of merit may make for a year, none of it is worth a quarter of bowing to the sincere.

question: Which stories have Sāriputta asking the Buddha to show his relatives or friends the way to the Brahma world?
title: The Story about the Brahmin Devahita
synopsis: When the Buddha was ill one time he asked for hot water from the Brahmin Devahita, who readily gave it; the Brahmin then asked to whom alms were best given, and the Buddha explained that his alms had great fruit, and then spoke the following verse about the true Brahmin.
verse_english: Dhp 423: One who knows their past lives, sees heaven and places of loss, and has attained the end of rebirth; a sage of perfect insight at the summit of spiritual perfection: that’s who I declare a brahmin. The Sayings of the Dhamma are complete.

verse_english: Dhp 107: Rather than serve the sacred flame in the forest for a hundred years, it’s better to honor for a single hour a personage who has developed themselves. That offering is better than the hundred year sacrifice.

title: The Story about the Hunter Koka’s Dogs
synopsis: The hunter Koka blamed a bhikkhu for his failure to catch game and he set his dogs on him, chasing him up a tree; the bhikkhu’s robe fell over the hunter and the dogs mistakenly devoured him instead; the bhikkhu worried whether his actions led to the death of the man, and the Buddha reassured him with a verse.
verse_english: Dhp 125: Whoever wrongs a man who has done no wrong, a pure man who has not a blemish, the evil backfires on the fool, like fine dust thrown upwind.

question: Which stories feature hunters?

question: Which stories feature hunters?

verse_english: Dhp 80: While irrigators guide water, fletchers bend arrows straight, and carpenters bend timber straight, the astute tame themselves.

verse_english: Dhp 83: True persons give up everything, they don’t cajole for the things they desire. Though touched by sadness or happiness, the astute appear neither depressed nor elated.

title: The Story about Kisā Gotamī
synopsis: Kisā Gotamī’s child died, but she did not believe it, and went round trying to find a cure; someone sent her to the Buddha who asked her to bring mustard seeds from a house that has never seen death; she was unable to, of course, and realised death is pervasive; the Buddha then taught her with a verse and she became a Stream-enterer.
verse_english: Dhp 287: As a mighty flood sweeps away a sleeping village, death steals away a man who dotes on children and cattle, his mind caught up in them.

title: The Story about Udena
synopsis: King Udena had two queens, Sāmāvatī, who was a follower of the Buddha, and Māgandiyā, who was spurned by the Buddha; out of jealousy Māgandiyā brought about the destruction of Sāmāvatī and her five hundred followers, all of whom had attained stages of Awakening; Māgandiyā and her family, who were full of defilements, were put to death by the king; when what had happened was reported to the Buddha he spoke some verses about them.
verse_english: Dhp 21: Heedfulness is the state free of death; heedlessness is the state of death. question: Which stories take place during a famine?

synopsis: The Buddha saw that a poor man was ready to attain Stream-entry, and went with the monastics to give him teachings; the man however spent the whole morning seeking his lost ox; the Buddha ordered that the tired man be fed first, and only later did he teach him; afterwards he spoke a verse to the monastics.
verse_english: Dhp 203: Hunger is the worst illness, conditions are the worst suffering. When one has known this as it is, extinguishment is the ultimate happiness.

question: Which stories take place during a famine?
title: The Story about Ascending the Ganges
synopsis: The Bodhisatta’s son in a previous life met some Paccekabuddhas, attained Awakening and later died; when his father found out he honoured his grave; through the power of that merit, when in this life he became the Buddha, he received similar great honours; he taught the monastics with a verse.
verse_english: Dhp 290: If by giving up material happiness one sees abundant happiness, the attentive would give up material happiness, seeing the abundant happiness.

question: Which stories centre on Mahā Kassapa?
title: The Story about the Elder Mahā Kassapa
synopsis: The Buddha set out on walkabout with a great host of bhikkhus, but seeing none left behind in Sāvatthī, he sent Elder Mahā Kassapa and his entourage back; some bhikkhus, not knowing about the instruction, accused the elder of being attached to his regular supporters, but the Buddha explained it was otherwise.
verse_english: Dhp 91: The mindful apply themselves; they delight in no abode. Like a swan gone from the marsh, they leave home after home behind.

question: Which stories centre on Mahā Kassapa?
title: The Story about Māra
synopsis: One night because of the arrival of several great elders Elder Rāhula, who was eight years old at the time, gave up his room and slept near the Buddha’s hut; Māra thought to frighten him and took the form of a great elephant and trumpeted near him; the Buddha explained with some verses that Elder Rāhula was an Arahat and was therefore unafraid.
verse_english: Dhp 351: One who is confident, unafraid, rid of craving, free of blemish, having struck down the arrows flying to future lives, this bag of bones is their last. / Dhp 352: Rid of craving, free of grasping, expert in the definition of terms, knowing the correct structure and sequence of syllables, they are said to be one who bears their final body, one of great wisdom, a great person.

question: Which stories centre on Mahā Kassapa?
title: The Story about Pasenadi Kosala
synopsis: King Pasenadi, at one time in his life, always overate and suffered the consequences of torpidity and drowsiness; he went to the Buddha who taught him with a verse; he also taught another verse for his attendant to recite which would remind the king not to eat so much.
verse_english: Dhp 325: One who gets drowsy from overeating, fond of sleep, rolling round the bed like a great hog stuffed with grain: that dullard returns to the womb again and again.

question: Which stories centre on Mahā Kassapa?
title: The Story about Jīvaka’s Question
synopsis: Devadatta hurled a rock down on the Buddha, which cut his foot; the Buddha’s physician Jīvaka applied medicine which needs to be applied for only a short time, but immediately thereafter he had to leave and was unable to return; the Buddha knew his thoughts though and asked Elder Ānanda to remove the medicine; the next day Jīvaka asked if the Buddha suffered pain because of his oversight, and the Buddha gave his reply in a verse.
verse_english: Dhp 90: At journey’s end, rid of sorrow; everywhere free, all ties given up, no fever is found in them.

question: Which stories centre on Mahā Kassapa?
title: The Story about the Devadhītā Lāja
synopsis: A young woman working in the fields gave parched rice to Elder Mahā Kassapa and was thereby reborn as a Devadhītā in Tusita Heaven; she desired to do more good deeds for Elder Mahā Kassapa, but was restrained by him; the Buddha explained the reason for her motivation with a verse.
verse_english: Dhp 118: If you do something good, do it again and again, set your heart on it, for piling up goodness is joyful.

question: Which stories centre on Mahā Kassapa?
title: The Story about the Elder Mahā Kassapa
synopsis: Elder Mahā Kassapa, after collecting his almsfood, sat in meditation and tried to understand in all its breadth the rising and falling away of living beings; the Buddha advised him that only Buddhas have such thorough knowledge, and then he spoke a verse.
verse_english: Dhp 28: When the astute dispel negligence by means of diligence, ascending the palace of wisdom, sorrowless, they behold this generation of sorrow, as an attentive one on a mountain top beholds the fools below.

question: Which stories centre on Mahā Kassapa?
title: The Story about the Elder Mahā Kassapa’s Pupil
synopsis: A faithless pupil of Elder Mahā Kassapa, after numerous other acts of deceit, tricked a supporter into giving him food and drinks which he said were needed by the elder; after being rebuked he burned down the elder’s hut, ran away and was later reborn in Avīci, the relentless hell; the Buddha then gave some advice in verse.
verse_english: Dhp 61: If while wandering you find no partner equal or better than yourself, then firmly resolve to wander alone— there’s no fellowship with fools.

question: Which stories centre on Mahā Kassapa?
title: The Story about Giving Alms to the Elder Mahā Kassapa
synopsis: Elder Mahā Kassapa rose from meditation after seven days and went for alms; celestial spirits stepped forward to donate to him but he dismissed them, then Sakka and his wife Sujā disguised themselves as weavers and succeeded in giving alms, but Elder Mahā Kassapa discovered who they were and chided them; the Buddha spoke a verse about him.
verse_english: Dhp 56: Faint is the fragrance of sandal or pinwheel; but the fragrance of the virtuous floats to the highest gods.

title: The Story about Three Groups
synopsis: Three different groups of bhikkhus who were on their way to the Buddha saw a crow die in mid-air, a woman drowned on a voyage and themselves get buried in a cave; they asked the Buddha why it all happened, and he explained there is nowhere to escape from the results of bad actions, and spoke a verse.
verse_english: Dhp 127: Not in midair, nor mid-ocean, nor hiding in a mountain cleft; you’ll find no place on the planet to escape your wicked deeds.

synopsis: Elder Upananda taught well, but was a greedy bhikkhu who always took the biggest offering, one day he swindled two bhikkhus out of a blanket, and the Buddha explained that one should train oneself before teaching to others, and summarised his teaching with a verse.
verse_english: Dhp 158: The astute would avoid being corrupted by first grounding themselves in what is suitable, and then instructing others.

question: In a past-life tale, a woman so attached to money comes back as a small animal living on top of the hoard. Which story?
title: The Story about the One Who Honoured Her Husband
synopsis: Patipūjikā passed away from heaven and was reborn on earth, had four sons, served the monastics faithfully, and at the end of her life was reunited with her husband Mālabhārī in Tāvatiṁsa Heaven; the monastics told the Buddha about the loss of their benefactor, and he gave this teaching.
verse_english: Dhp 48: The terminator gains control of the man who has not had his fill of pleasures, even as he gathers flowers, his mind caught up in them.

verse_english: Dhp 47: As a mighty flood sweeps off a sleeping village, death steals away a man even as he gathers flowers, his mind caught up in them.

verse_english: Dhp 130: All tremble at the rod, all love life. Treating others like oneself, neither kill nor incite to kill.

title: The Story about the Group of Six

verse_english: Dhp 129: All tremble at the rod, all fear death. Treating others like oneself, neither kill nor incite to kill.

title: The Story about Udena
synopsis: King Udena had two queens, Sāmāvatī, who was a follower of the Buddha, and Māgandiyā, who was spurned by the Buddha; out of jealousy Māgandiyā brought about the destruction of Sāmāvatī and her five hundred followers, all of whom had attained stages of Awakening; Māgandiyā and her family, who were full of defilements, were put to death by the king; when what had happened was reported to the Buddha he spoke some verses about them.
verse_english: Dhp 21: Heedfulness is the state free of death; heedlessness is the state of death. The heedful do not die, while the heedless are like the dead. / Dhp 22: Understanding this distinction when it comes to heedfulness, the astute rejoice in heedfulness, happy in the noble ones’ domain. / Dhp 23: They who regularly meditate, always staunchly vigorous; the attentive realize extinguishment, the supreme sanctuary from the yoke.

question: Kokasunakhaluddakavatthu
title: The Story about Kokālika
synopsis: Elder Kokālika once spent the Rains Retreat with the two Chief Disciples, but was not honoured as they were, and then went about abusing them, saying they were full of defilements; the Buddha tried to restrain him but he fell into the Lotus Niraya Hell; the Buddha then explained how a bhikkhu should behave with a verse.
verse_english: Dhp 363: When a mendicant of restrained mouth, thoughtful in counsel, not restless, explains the text and its meaning, their words are sweet.

question: Kokasunakhaluddakavatthu
title: The Story about the Hunter Koka’s Dogs
synopsis: The hunter Koka blamed a bhikkhu for his failure to catch game and he set his dogs on him, chasing him up a tree; the bhikkhu’s robe fell over the hunter and the dogs mistakenly devoured him instead; the bhikkhu worried whether his actions led to the death of the man, and the Buddha reassured him with a verse.
verse_english: Dhp 125: Whoever wrongs a man who has done no wrong, a pure man who has not a blemish, the evil backfires on the fool, like fine dust thrown upwind.

question: Kokasunakhaluddakavatthu
title: The Story about Devadatta
synopsis: Elder Sāriputta taught on generosity and people decided to give alms; one man gave a robe, which they decided to give to Elder Devadatta; when the Buddha heard about it he related a Birth Story about Devadatta, who, as an elephant hunter, disguised himself as a Paccekabuddha in order to kill his prey, and then spoke some verses about him.
verse_english: Dhp 9: One who, not free of stains themselves, would wear the robe stained in ocher, bereft of self-control and truth: they are not worthy of the ocher robe. / Dhp 10: One who’s purged all their stains, steady in ethics, possessed of self-control and of truth, they are truly worthy of the ocher robe.

question: Kokasunakhaluddakavatthu
title: The Story about the Elder Uppalavaṇṇā
synopsis: After the rape of Elder Uppalavaṇṇā the bhikkhus were discussing whether those who had become an Arahat still enjoyed the pleasures of the flesh; when this was reported to the Buddha he said it was not so, and – affirming her purity of mind – he spoke a verse explaining the situation.
verse_english: Dhp 401: Like water from a lotus leaf, like a mustard seed off the point of a pin, sensual pleasures slip off them: that’s who I declare a brahmin.

question: Kokasunakhaluddakavatthu
title: The Story about Five Hundred Youths
synopsis: Fifty youths were going out of Rājagaha carrying baskets of cakes, but did not think to offer any to the Buddha and the bhikkhus, until they saw Elder Mahā Kassapa, and then they offered him the cakes; the Buddha spoke a verse about Elder Mahā Kassapa.
verse_english: Dhp 217: One accomplished in virtue and vision, firmly principled, and truthful, doing oneself what ought be done: that’s who the people love.

question: Kokasunakhaluddakavatthu
title: The Story about Pasedani Kosala
synopsis: King Pasenadi was always overeating and suffering for it so the Buddha had the king’s nephew learn and recite a verse which reminded the king to be moderate; later the king told the Buddha he was cured, and the Buddha recited a verse.
verse_english: Dhp 204: Health is the ultimate blessing; contentment, the ultimate wealth; trust is the ultimate family; extinguishment, the ultimate happiness.

question: Kokasunakhaluddakavatthu
title: The Story about Pasenadi Kosala
synopsis: King Pasenadi, at one time in his life, always overate and suffered the consequences of torpidity and drowsiness; he went to the Buddha who taught him with a verse; he also taught another verse for his attendant to recite which would remind the king not to eat so much.
verse_english: Dhp 325: One who gets drowsy from overeating, fond of sleep, rolling round the bed like a great hog stuffed with grain: that dullard returns to the womb again and again.

question: Kokasunakhaluddakavatthu
title: The Story about Those from Kosambī
synopsis: Parallels: Ja 428; Vin Mv 10.1-5; Ud 4.5; Ja 37124 The followers of two bhikkhus of Kosambī fell into a dispute and despite the Buddha’s admonitions, refused to be reconciled; the Buddha went forth to Pārileyyaka forest and was served by an elephant and a monkey; meanwhile the lay people refused to attend on the bhikkhus till they came to their senses; eventually they asked for forgiveness and the Buddha taught them with a verse. Kosala, Prince Dīghāvu, Bālaka, Elder Bhagu, Anāthapiṇḍika, Visākhā
verse_english: Dhp 6: When others do not understand, let us, who do understand this, restrain ourselves in this regard; for that is how conflicts are laid to rest.

question: Kokasunakhaluddakavatthu
title: The Story about Culla Sāri
synopsis: Elder Culla Sāri gave medical treatment to others in exchange for a portion of food, which is against the right ways of earning his livelihood as laid down by the Buddha; when the Buddha heard of his behaviour he gave a teaching in some verses.
verse_english: Dhp 244: Life is easy for the shameless. With all the rude courage of a crow, they live pushy, rude, and corrupt. / Dhp 245: Life is hard for the conscientious, always seeking purity, neither clinging nor rude, pure of livelihood and discerning.

question: Is punishment for cruelty limited to this lifetime?
title: The Story about the Yakkhinī Kāḷi
synopsis: A barren woman brings home a young woman for her husband, but every time the young wife conceives the barren wife contrives an abortion; through life after life they consume each other’s children, until brought to the Buddha, who taught them with a verse. named, Elder Ānanda, Deva Sumana
verse_english: Dhp 5: For never is hatred laid to rest by hate, it’s laid to rest by love: this is an ancient teaching.

question: Is punishment for cruelty limited to this lifetime?
title: The Story about the Ājīvaka Jambuka
synopsis: For many years the Ājīvaka Jambuka ate excrement and slept on the floor yet convinced his devotees that he only ate food from a grass-tip and never slept, until the Buddha confronted him with his deceit; Jambuka repented, ordained and soon became an Arahat; the Buddha spoke a verse to Jambuka’s devotees. Brahma
verse_english: Dhp 70: Month after month a fool may eat food from a grass-blade’s tip; but they’ll never be worth a sixteenth part of one who has appraised the teaching.

question: Is punishment for cruelty limited to this lifetime?
title: The Story about a Company of Boys
verse_english: Dhp 131: Creatures love happiness, so if you harm them with a stick in search of your own happiness, after death you won’t find happiness. / Dhp 132: Creatures love happiness, so if you don’t harm them with a stick in search of your own happiness, after death you will find happiness.

question: Is punishment for cruelty limited to this lifetime?
title: The Story about the Python Peta
synopsis: A leading supporter of the Buddha Kassapa recognised a thief as such, and the scoundrel conceived a grudge which led him to commit many wicked deeds, including burning his fields and burning down the Perfumed Cottage; he went to Niraya Hell and was later reborn in the world of the Petas where Elder Moggallāna saw him; the Buddha explained how he got there, and spoke a verse.
verse_english: Dhp 136: The fool does not understand the evil that they do. But because of those deeds, that simpleton is tormented as if burnt by fire.

question: Is punishment for cruelty limited to this lifetime?
title: The Story about Devadatta
synopsis: Devadatta grew jealous and plotted to kill the Buddha, when that failed he tried to cause a schism; eventually he wished to seek for forgiveness, but before he reached the Buddha he fell into Avīci, the hell of relentless suffering; the Buddha summarised the events with a verse. Sāriputta, Elder Mahā Moggallāna, Elder Kokālika
verse_english: Dhp 17: Here they’re tormented, hereafter they’re tormented, an evildoer is tormented in both places. They’re tormented thinking of bad things they’ve done; when gone to a bad place, they’re tormented all the more.

question: Is punishment for cruelty limited to this lifetime?
title: The Story about the Pig Butcher Cunda
synopsis: Cunda was a cruel pig butcher who cared not for the suffering he inflicted, and did no good deeds at all; before he died he started behaving like a pig himself, and later fell into Avīci, the hell of relentless suffering; the Buddha summarised the events with a verse.
verse_english: Dhp 15: Here they grieve, hereafter they grieve, an evildoer grieves in both places. They grieve and fret, seeing their own corrupt deeds.

question: Is punishment for cruelty limited to this lifetime?
title: The Story about a Certain Man
synopsis: King Pasenadi was overcome with desire for another man’s wife and sought to have him killed; during the night he woke to the sound of four people screaming; the Buddha explained they were adulterers in their previous lives and did no good deeds, and then he spoke a verse.
verse_english: Dhp 60: Long is the night for the wakeful; long is the league for the weary; long transmigrate the fools who don’t understand the true teaching.

question: Is punishment for cruelty limited to this lifetime?
title: The Story about Two Monastic Friends
synopsis: Two friends ordained, one followed the path of practice and soon attained; the other the path of study and became puffed up with pride; the Buddha showed how the one who attained could answer his questions much better than the one who studied, and he spoke some verses about them.
verse_english: Dhp 19: Much though they may recite scripture, if a negligent person does not apply them, then, like a cowherd who counts the cattle of others, they miss out on the blessings of the ascetic life. / Dhp 20: Little though they may recite scripture, if they live in line with the teaching, having given up greed, hate, and delusion, with deep understanding and heart well freed, not grasping to this life or the next, they share in the blessings of the ascetic life.

question: Is punishment for cruelty limited to this lifetime?
title: The Story about the Lay Disciple Mahā Kāla
synopsis: The householder Mahā Kāla listened to an all-night Dhamma teaching at Jetavana, but in the morning was beaten to death by people who mistook him for a thief; the Buddha explained that he had caused the unjust death of another in a previous life, and his bad deed had caught up with him, and gave a teaching in a verse.
verse_english: Dhp 161: For the evil that is done by oneself, born and produced in oneself, grinds down a simpleton, as diamond grinds a lesser gem.

question: Is punishment for cruelty limited to this lifetime?
title: The Story about Khema
synopsis: One of the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika’s nephews, Khema, was so handsome all the women fell in love with him, and he was frequently caught in adultery; the king didn’t punish Khema, due to his affection for his father, so his father took his son to the Buddha who taught him in some verses the destiny of those who dally with other men’s wives.
verse_english: Dhp 309: Four things befall a heedless man who sleeps with another’s wife: wickedness, poor sleep, ill-repute, and rebirth in hell. / Dhp 310: He accrues wickedness and is reborn in a bad place, all so a frightened couple may snatch a moment’s pleasure, for which rulers impose a heavy punishment. That’s why a man should not sleep with another’s wife.

question: Can knowledge actually be dangerous in the hands of a foolish person?
title: The Story about the Elder Udāyī
synopsis: Elder Udāyī lived with the Buddha, but when questioned by visiting bhikkhus it was found he did not know even the fundamentals of the teaching; they told this to the Buddha, who spoke a verse.
verse_english: Dhp 64: Though a fool attends to the wise even for the rest of their life, they still don’t understand the teaching, like a spoon the taste of the soup.

question: Can knowledge actually be dangerous in the hands of a foolish person?
title: The Story about the Thieves Who Broke Their Bonds
synopsis: Two thieves went to listen to the Dhamma; one of them attained a stage of Awakening, the other managed to undo a knot in someone’s clothes and steal some pennies; when this was reported to the Buddha he spoke a verse in explanation.
verse_english: Dhp 63: The fool who thinks they’re a fool is wise at least to that extent. But the true fool is said to be one who imagines that they are wise.

question: Can knowledge actually be dangerous in the hands of a foolish person?
title: The Story about the Peta with Sixty Hammers
synopsis: A young man learned the art of stone-throwing, but used it to kill a Paccekabuddha; he was reborn in Avīci, the hell of relentless suffering, and later as a Peta whose head was constantly crushed by sixty hammers; the Buddha explained what happens to fools who gain knowledge with a verse.
verse_english: Dhp 72: Whatever fame a fool may get, it only gives rise to harm. Whatever good features they have it ruins, and blows their head into bits.

question: Can knowledge actually be dangerous in the hands of a foolish person?
title: The Story about the Fool’s Festival
synopsis: During a seven-day festival of fools in Sāvatthī the people used to go round insulting and disrespecting everyone they met; the Buddha’s supporters asked him to stay at the monastery for the duration and they sent almsfood there; this is the teaching the Buddha gave them when it was over.
verse_english: Dhp 26: Fools and simpletons devote themselves to negligence. But the wise protect diligence as their best treasure. / Dhp 27: Don’t devote yourself to negligence, or delight in erotic intimacy. For if you’re diligent and meditate, you’ll attain abundant happiness.

question: Why am I blind to my own shortcomings yet quick to judge everybody else?
title: The Story about the Sectarian Disciples
synopsis: Some children of the families of sectarians were forbidden to go to Jetavana, but when thirst overtook them one day they went anyway; the Buddha gave them an appropriate teaching and they converted; later they went to the monastery to ordain and the Buddha taught them with some verses.
verse_english: Dhp 318: Seeing fault where there is none, and blind to the actual fault, beings who uphold wrong view go to a bad place. / Dhp 319: Knowing a fault as a fault and the faultless as faultless, beings who uphold right view go to a good place.

question: Why am I blind to my own shortcomings yet quick to judge everybody else?
title: The Story about the Elder Ujjhānasaññī
synopsis: Elder Ujjhānasaññī was always finding fault with the others, so the bhikkhus asked the Buddha about it; he remarked that one who is scrupulous is doing well, but one who enjoys finding fault, makes no progress, and he taught them with a verse.
verse_english: Dhp 253: When you look for the flaws of others, always finding fault, your defilements only grow, you’re far from ending defilements.

question: Why am I blind to my own shortcomings yet quick to judge everybody else?
title: The Story about the Nigaṇṭhas
synopsis: Some bhikkhus saw the Nigaṇṭhas and spoke of them as having some modesty as they wear a small covering at the front, the Nigaṇṭhas however declared they do so not out of modesty, but to protect the lives of dust-beings; when reported to the Buddha he spoke a verse about them.
verse_english: Dhp 316: Unashamed of what is shameful, ashamed of what is not shameful; beings who uphold wrong view go to a bad place. / Dhp 317: Seeing danger where there is none, and blind to the actual danger, beings who uphold wrong view go to a bad place.

question: Why am I blind to my own shortcomings yet quick to judge everybody else?
title: The Story about the Rich Man Meṇḍaka
synopsis: The rich man Meṇḍaka wanted to see the Buddha when he was passing through, but the outside ascetics tried to persuade him not to by telling him falsely that he teaches there is no result of actions; Meṇḍaka went anyway and the Buddha taught him with a verse. Vipassī, Avaroja
verse_english: Dhp 252: It’s easy to see the faults of others, hard to see one’s own. For the faults of others are tossed high like hay, while one’s own are hidden, as a cheat hides a bad hand.

question: Can you have insight without meditating, or meditation without insight?
title: The Story about the Elder Poṭhila
synopsis: Elder Poṭhila had been a reciter of the Three Baskets under all seven Buddhas, but had never truly put the teaching into practice, so the Buddha started calling him Empty Poṭhila; taking the hint he went far away to practice meditation, and later the Buddha appeared to him and spoke a verse to encourage him.
verse_english: Dhp 282: From meditation springs wisdom, without meditation, wisdom ends. Knowing these two paths— of progress and decline— you should conduct yourself so that wisdom grows.

question: Can you have insight without meditating, or meditation without insight?
title: The Story about the Elder Khāṇu Koṇḍañña
synopsis: Elder Khāṇu Koṇḍañña, sitting in meditation, was unmoved when five hundred thieves piled up their stolen goods all over him at night; the thieves, impressed with his equanimity, converted and were ordained; the Buddha gave a teaching in a verse on that occasion.
verse_english: Dhp 111: Better to live a single day wise and absorbed in meditation than to live a hundred years witless and lacking immersion.

question: Can you have insight without meditating, or meditation without insight?
title: The Story about a Company of Bhikkhus
synopsis: During a visit by thirty bhikkhus who had come in from the countryside, Elder Sāriputta, believing they were ready to become Arahats, asked the Buddha to explain what were the two things he had heard spoken about, and the Buddha told they were calm and insight, and exhorted the bhikkhus with a verse.
verse_english: Dhp 384: When a brahmin has gone beyond dualistic phenomena, then they consciously make an end of all fetters.

question: Can you have insight without meditating, or meditation without insight?
title: The Story about a Company of Bhikkhus
synopsis: After Soṇa Kūṭikaṇṇa received ordination he recited Dhamma to the Buddha who praised him for it, which also caused the Devas to rejoice; on hearing about it, Soṇa’s mother invited her son to teach her Dhamma also, and wouldn’t leave the teaching even when she heard nine hundred thieves had broken into her house; seeing her piety, the thieves converted and went forth; this is the teaching the Buddha gave at that time.
verse_english: Dhp 368: A mendicant who meditates on love, devoted to the Buddha’s teaching, would realize the peaceful state, the blissful stilling of conditions. / Dhp 369: Bail out this boat, mendicant! When bailed out it will float lightly. Having cut off desire and hate, you shall reach extinguishment. / Dhp 370: Five to cut, five to drop, and five more to develop. When a mendicant slips five chains they’re said to have crossed the flood. / Dhp 371: Practice absorption, don’t be negligent! Don’t let the mind delight in the senses! Don’t heedlessly swallow a hot iron ball! And when it burns, don’t cry, “Oh, the pain!” / Dhp 372: No absorption for one without wisdom, no wisdom for one without absorption. But one with absorption and wisdom— they have truly drawn near to extinguishment. / Dhp 373: A mendicant who enters an empty hut with mind at peace finds a superhuman delight as they rightly discern the Dhamma. / Dhp 374: Whenever they are mindful of the rise and fall of the aggregates, they feel rapture and joy: that is freedom from death for one who knows. / Dhp 375: This is the very start of the path for a wise mendicant here: guarding the senses, contentment, and restraint in the monastic code. / Dhp 376: Mix with spiritual friends, who are tireless and pure of livelihood. Share what you have with others, being skillful in your conduct. And when you’re full of joy, you’ll make an end to suffering.

question: Can you have insight without meditating, or meditation without insight?
title: The Story about the Elder Who Meditated on a Mirage
synopsis: A bhikkhu who had been practising meditation saw a mirage, and realised this was similar to existence; he next saw froth on a river, with its bubbles bursting, and he realised existence is the same; the Buddha summed up his insight with a verse.
verse_english: Dhp 46: Knowing this body’s like foam, realizing it’s all just a mirage, and cutting off Māra’s blossoming, vanish from the King of Death.

question: Can you have insight without meditating, or meditation without insight?
title: The Story about the Twin Miracle
synopsis: After spending his seventh Rains Retreat teaching the Abhidhamma in the Realm of the Thirty-Three, the Buddha descended on a staircase built by Sakka, the Lord of the Devas, and Elder Sāriputta praised the Buddha in his glory; the Buddha explained the matter by reciting a verse. Bimbisāra, King Pasenadi Kosala, Sakka, Gaṇḍa, Elder Ānanda, Devaputta Vātavalāhaka, Devaputta Sun, Pūraṇa Kassapa, Gharaṇī, Culla Anāthapiṇḍika, Mahā Brahma, Sāmaṇerī Cīrā, Sāmaṇera Cunda, Bhikkhunī Uppalavaṇṇā, Nandivisāla, Elder Anuruddha, Culla Anāthapiṇḍika, Deva Indaka, Deva Aṅkura, Buddha Kassapa, Deva Pañcasikha, Mātali the charioteer, Suyāma Lives, Previous Buddhas, Bodhisatta
verse_english: Dhp 181: The attentive intent on absorption, who love the peace of renunciation, the Buddhas, ever mindful, are envied by even the gods.

question: Is there an image of pride and hatred falling away like a tiny grain slipping off a sharp point?
title: The Story about the Five Hundred Bhikkhus
synopsis: Five hundred bhikkhus who had received instructions from the Buddha saw jasmine flowers fading away and determined to attain Awakening before the flowers dropped from the stems; the Buddha projected an image of himself and gave them this teaching, after hearing which, they became Arahats.
verse_english: Dhp 377: As a jasmine sheds its withered flowers, O mendicants, shed greed and hate.

question: Is there an image of pride and hatred falling away like a tiny grain slipping off a sharp point?
title: The Story about the Elder Mahā Panthaka
synopsis: When Elder Culla Panthaka could not remember even one verse even after three months of trying, and his elder brother, Elder Mahā Panthaka, asked him to leave the monastery, the bhikkhus could not believe Elder Mahā Panthaka had not been angry with his brother, but the Buddha confirmed his purity with a verse.
verse_english: Dhp 407: They’ve discarded greed and hate, along with conceit and contempt, like a mustard seed off the point of a pin: that’s who I declare a brahmin.

question: Is there an image of pride and hatred falling away like a tiny grain slipping off a sharp point?
title: The Story about a Company of Bhikkhus
synopsis: Some learned bhikkhus, jealous of other bhikkhus having disciples who carried out their duties for them, went to the Buddha and asked for others to be forbidden to teach until they had undertaken training under their tutelage; the Buddha understood their intentions and taught them with a verse.
verse_english: Dhp 262: Not by mere enunciation, or a beautiful complexion does a person become holy, if they’re jealous, stingy, and devious. / Dhp 263: But if they’ve cut that out, dug it up at the root, eradicated it, that intelligent one, purged of vice, is said to be holy.

question: Is there an image of pride and hatred falling away like a tiny grain slipping off a sharp point?
title: The Story about the Elder Uppalavaṇṇā
synopsis: After the rape of Elder Uppalavaṇṇā the bhikkhus were discussing whether those who had become an Arahat still enjoyed the pleasures of the flesh; when this was reported to the Buddha he said it was not so, and – affirming her purity of mind – he spoke a verse explaining the situation.
verse_english: Dhp 401: Like water from a lotus leaf, like a mustard seed off the point of a pin, sensual pleasures slip off them: that’s who I declare a brahmin.

question: A monk kept chanting sad songs at weddings and happy ones at funerals. What verse did the Buddha give?
title: The Story about the Vajjian Bhikkhu
synopsis: A Vajjian prince ordained, but hearing music and festivities coming from Vesālī, he was dissatisfied and asked: ‘Who is worse off than we monastics?’ The Buddha taught him the various kinds of suffering there are in births and deaths with some verses.
verse_english: Dhp 302: Going forth is hard, it’s hard to be happy; life at home is hard too, and painful, it’s painful to stay when you’ve nothing in common. A traveler is a prey to pain, so don’t be a traveler, don’t be prey to pain.

question: A monk kept chanting sad songs at weddings and happy ones at funerals. What verse did the Buddha give?
title: The Story about the Lay Disciple Dhammika
synopsis: Dhammika, a good supporter, lay dying and he requested the bhikkhus to chant the Mindfulness discourse for him; seeing celestial chariots coming to take him away, he asked them to wait until the bhikkhus finished chanting, but the bhikkhus thought he was asking them to stop and go away; later the Buddha explained Dhammika was reborn in the Tusita Heaven and he spoke a verse about him.
verse_english: Dhp 16: Here they rejoice, hereafter they rejoice, one who does good rejoices in both places. They rejoice and celebrate, seeing their own pure deeds.

question: A monk kept chanting sad songs at weddings and happy ones at funerals. What verse did the Buddha give?
title: The Story about a Company of Bhikkhus
synopsis: The bhikkhus discussed what is the true good in the world, some said ruling, some said love, some said food; the Buddha explained that those things are within the realm of suffering, and then he pointed out what is truly good with a verse.
verse_english: Dhp 194: Happy, the arising of Buddhas! Happy, the teaching of Dhamma! Happy is the harmony of the Saṅgha, and the striving of the harmonious is happy.

question: A monk kept chanting sad songs at weddings and happy ones at funerals. What verse did the Buddha give?
title: The Story about the Elder Kuṇḍalakesī
synopsis: Kuṇḍalakesī, who had previously killed her husband and joined the wanderers and expertly defended their doctrines, was converted by Elder Sāriputta with a simple teaching; the bhikkhus wondered how, and the Buddha spoke some verses to explain it.
verse_english: Dhp 102: Better than reciting a hundred meaningless verses is a single saying of Dhamma, hearing which brings you peace. / Dhp 103: The supreme conqueror is not he who conquers a million men in battle, but he who conquers a single man: himself.

question: A monk kept chanting sad songs at weddings and happy ones at funerals. What verse did the Buddha give?
title: The Story about a Certain Maiden of Family
synopsis: The Buddha and the monastics were invited to a wedding, and the bride served them with all due attention; the groom, however, was overcome with lust and could pay no attention to his duties; the Buddha spoke a verse to him.
verse_english: Dhp 202: There is no fire like greed, no crime like hate, no suffering like the aggregates, no bliss beyond peace.

question: A monk kept chanting sad songs at weddings and happy ones at funerals. What verse did the Buddha give?
title: The Story about the Elder Vakkali
synopsis: Elder Vakkali was obsessed with the Buddha’s body and even gave up his meditation to spend his time gazing at the Buddha; the Buddha sent him to spend the Rains Retreat elsewhere, and he was on the verge of suicide when the Buddha appeared to him and his sorrow vanished; the Buddha then taught him with a verse.
verse_english: Dhp 381: A monk full of joy trusting in the Buddha’s teaching, would realize the peaceful state, the blissful stilling of conditions.

question: A monk kept chanting sad songs at weddings and happy ones at funerals. What verse did the Buddha give?
title: The Story about the Elder Lāḷudāyi
synopsis: The bhikkhu Lāḷudāyi was always reciting the wrong verses – dirges at weddings, and joyful verses at funerals, and so on; the Buddha explained that he did the very same in a past life and spoke a verse.
verse_english: Dhp 152: A person of little learning ages like an ox— their flesh grows, but not their wisdom.

question: When the Buddha announced he would die soon, one monk went off alone to meditate instead of crowding round him. How did the Buddha react?
title: The Story about the Elder Vanavāsī Tissa
synopsis: The seven year old boy Tissa ordained under Elder Sāriputta, and later, spurning gains and the attentions of his relatives, went forth into solitude, and quickly became an Arahat; the Buddha spoke a verse about him. (Piṇḍapātadāyaka Tissa, Kambaladāyaka Tissa), Brahmin Mahāsena, Elder Sāriputta, Elder Mahā Moggallāna, Upasāḷhaka, Elder Ānanda
verse_english: Dhp 75: For the means to profit and the path to quenching are two quite different things. A mendicant disciple of the Buddha, understanding what this really means, would never delight in honors, but rather would foster seclusion.

question: When the Buddha announced he would die soon, one monk went off alone to meditate instead of crowding round him. How did the Buddha react?
title: The Story about a Company of Bhikkhus
synopsis: After Soṇa Kūṭikaṇṇa received ordination he recited Dhamma to the Buddha who praised him for it, which also caused the Devas to rejoice; on hearing about it, Soṇa’s mother invited her son to teach her Dhamma also, and wouldn’t leave the teaching even when she heard nine hundred thieves had broken into her house; seeing her piety, the thieves converted and went forth; this is the teaching the Buddha gave at that time.
verse_english: Dhp 368: A mendicant who meditates on love, devoted to the Buddha’s teaching, would realize the peaceful state, the blissful stilling of conditions. / Dhp 369: Bail out this boat, mendicant! When bailed out it will float lightly. Having cut off desire and hate, you shall reach extinguishment. / Dhp 370: Five to cut, five to drop, and five more to develop. When a mendicant slips five chains they’re said to have crossed the flood. / Dhp 371: Practice absorption, don’t be negligent! Don’t let the mind delight in the senses! Don’t heedlessly swallow a hot iron ball! And when it burns, don’t cry, “Oh, the pain!” / Dhp 372: No absorption for one without wisdom, no wisdom for one without absorption. But one with absorption and wisdom— they have truly drawn near to extinguishment. / Dhp 373: A mendicant who enters an empty hut with mind at peace finds a superhuman delight as they rightly discern the Dhamma. / Dhp 374: Whenever they are mindful of the rise and fall of the aggregates, they feel rapture and joy: that is freedom from death for one who knows. / Dhp 375: This is the very start of the path for a wise mendicant here: guarding the senses, contentment, and restraint in the monastic code. / Dhp 376: Mix with spiritual friends, who are tireless and pure of livelihood. Share what you have with others, being skillful in your conduct. And when you’re full of joy, you’ll make an end to suffering.

question: When the Buddha announced he would die soon, one monk went off alone to meditate instead of crowding round him. How did the Buddha react?
title: The Story about Elder Meghiya
synopsis: The Buddha’s attendant Meghiya left the Buddha alone against his wishes, and went and meditated in a mango grove; his mind was overcome with defilements and the Buddha taught him with some verses at the conclusion of which he attained Stream-entry.
verse_english: Dhp 33: The mind quivers and shakes, hard to guard, hard to curb. The discerning straighten it out, like a fletcher an arrow. / Dhp 34: Like a fish pulled from the sea and cast upon the shore, this mind flounders about, trying to throw off Māra’s dominion.

question: When the Buddha announced he would die soon, one monk went off alone to meditate instead of crowding round him. How did the Buddha react?
title: The Story about the Elder Tissa
synopsis: When Elder Tissa heard the Buddha declare his intention to finally pass away in four months time, rather than attend on the Buddha, he went to the forest to practice the teaching; the Buddha lauded him and said this is how one truly honours him, and spoke a verse.
verse_english: Dhp 205: Having drunk the nectar of seclusion and the nectar of peace— free of stress, free of evil, drink the joyous nectar of truth.

question: When the Buddha announced he would die soon, one monk went off alone to meditate instead of crowding round him. How did the Buddha react?
title: The Story about the Elder Dhammārāma
synopsis: When Elder Dhammārāma heard the Buddha declare his intention to finally pass away in four months time, rather than attend on the Buddha, he went to the forest to practice the teaching; the Buddha lauded him and said this is how one truly honours him, and spoke a verse.
verse_english: Dhp 364: Delighting in the teaching, enjoying the teaching, contemplating the teaching, a mendicant who recollects the teaching doesn’t fall away from the true teaching.

question: When the Buddha announced he would die soon, one monk went off alone to meditate instead of crowding round him. How did the Buddha react?
title: The Story about Those from Kosambī
synopsis: Parallels: Ja 428; Vin Mv 10.1-5; Ud 4.5; Ja 37124 The followers of two bhikkhus of Kosambī fell into a dispute and despite the Buddha’s admonitions, refused to be reconciled; the Buddha went forth to Pārileyyaka forest and was served by an elephant and a monkey; meanwhile the lay people refused to attend on the bhikkhus till they came to their senses; eventually they asked for forgiveness and the Buddha taught them with a verse. Kosala, Prince Dīghāvu, Bālaka, Elder Bhagu, Anāthapiṇḍika, Visākhā
verse_english: Dhp 6: When others do not understand, let us, who do understand this, restrain ourselves in this regard; for that is how conflicts are laid to rest.

question: When the Buddha announced he would die soon, one monk went off alone to meditate instead of crowding round him. How did the Buddha react?
title: The Story about the Elder Vakkali
synopsis: Elder Vakkali was obsessed with the Buddha’s body and even gave up his meditation to spend his time gazing at the Buddha; the Buddha sent him to spend the Rains Retreat elsewhere, and he was on the verge of suicide when the Buddha appeared to him and his sorrow vanished; the Buddha then taught him with a verse.
verse_english: Dhp 381: A monk full of joy trusting in the Buddha’s teaching, would realize the peaceful state, the blissful stilling of conditions.

question: When the Buddha announced he would die soon, one monk went off alone to meditate instead of crowding round him. How did the Buddha react?
title: The Story about a Company of Bhikkhus
synopsis: Owing to the Kosambī bhikkhus falling into an argument, the Buddha went to Pārileyyaka forest and was served by an elephant; after the Rains Retreat Elder Ānanda, being urged by the great disciples, went to invite the Buddha to return to Sāvatthi; the Buddha explained that he had a good companion in the elephant, but without such-like it is better to live alone, and he spoke some verses.
verse_english: Dhp 328: If you find an alert companion, an attentive friend to live happily together, then, overcoming all adversities, wander with them, joyful and mindful. / Dhp 329: If you find no alert companion, no attentive friend to live happily together, then, like a king who flees his conquered realm, wander alone like a tusker in the wilds. / Dhp 330: It’s better to wander alone, there’s no fellowship with fools. Wander alone and do no wrong, at ease like a tusker in the wilds.

question: When the Buddha announced he would die soon, one monk went off alone to meditate instead of crowding round him. How did the Buddha react?
title: The Story about the Elder Attadattha
synopsis: When Elder Attadattha heard the Buddha declare his intention to finally pass away in four months time, rather than attend on the Buddha, he went to the forest to practice the teaching; the Buddha lauded him and said this is how one truly honours him, and spoke a verse.
verse_english: Dhp 166: Never neglect what is good for yourself for the sake of another, however great. Knowing well what is good for yourself, be intent upon your heart’s goal.

question: A young novice's mother talked him out of quitting monastic life. What teaching was he given?
title: The Story about the Novice Sāṇu
synopsis: Sānu was a novice who, when he recited the texts, attracted even the Devas to listen, but when he reached manhood he grew discontent and purposed to disrobe; his mother persuaded him to continue in the monastic life and take his higher ordination; this is the teaching the Buddha gave urging him to control his thoughts.
verse_english: Dhp 326: In the past my mind wandered how it wished, where it liked, as it pleased. Now I’ll carefully guide it, as a trainer with a hook guides a rutting elephant.

question: A young novice's mother talked him out of quitting monastic life. What teaching was he given?
title: The Story about the Novice Sukha
synopsis: The novice Sukha saw that irrigators, fletchers and carpenters mastered the objects they worked with, and realised that, if they can master unconscious things, he could master his mind; he asked his teacher Elder Sāriputta to bring his food, and by striving alone he became an Arahat; the Buddha then spoke a verse about him. Disciples, Mastery, Past Lives
verse_english: Dhp 145: While irrigators guide water, fletchers bend arrows straight, and carpenters bend timber straight, those true to their vows tame themselves.

question: A young novice's mother talked him out of quitting monastic life. What teaching was he given?
title: The Story about the Novice Sumana
synopsis: Elder Anuruddha gave the young boy Sumana the going-forth and he soon became an Arahat; through his power the novice overcame a Nāga who then became his servant; when bhikkhus who did not know who he was started making fun of the novice the Buddha decided to let him demonstrate his power and sent him to Lake Anotatta in the Himalayas to bring water; the Buddha pointed him out flying through the air and spoke a verse. the Sakyan, Mahānāma, Elder Anuruddha, Mahā Muṇḍa, Mahā Sumana, Culla Sumana, Paṇṇaka, Sakka, Suyāma, Santusita, Paranimmitavasavattī, Elder Ānanda
verse_english: Dhp 382: A young mendicant devoted to the Buddha’s teaching, lights up the world, like the moon freed from clouds.

question: A young novice's mother talked him out of quitting monastic life. What teaching was he given?
title: The Story about the Edler Ānanda’s Question about the Observance Day
synopsis: Elder Ānanda asked the Buddha to explain how the previous Buddhas had kept the Observance Day; he explained that although they held them after different lengths of time, the verses they recited were always the same, and he recited them. Kakusandha, Buddha Koṇāgamana, Buddha Kassapa
verse_english: Dhp 183: Not to do any evil; to embrace the good; to purify one’s mind: this is the instruction of the Buddhas. / Dhp 184: Patient acceptance is the ultimate fervor. Extinguishment is the ultimate, say the Buddhas. No true renunciate injures another, nor does an ascetic hurt another. / Dhp 185: Not speaking ill nor doing harm; restraint in the monastic code; moderation in eating; staying in remote lodgings; commitment to the higher mind— this is the instruction of the Buddhas.

question: A young novice's mother talked him out of quitting monastic life. What teaching was he given?
title: The Story about the Novice Paṇḍita
synopsis: The novice Paṇḍita saw that irrigators, fletchers and carpenters mastered the objects they worked with, and realised that if they can master unconscious things, he could master his mind; by striving he did just that and became an Arahat; the Buddha then spoke a verse about him. Sāriputta
verse_english: Dhp 80: While irrigators guide water, fletchers bend arrows straight, and carpenters bend timber straight, the astute tame themselves.

title: The Story about the Elder Vakkali

verse_english: Dhp 381: A monk full of joy trusting in the Buddha’s teaching, would realize the peaceful state, the blissful stilling of conditions.

question: A young novice's mother talked him out of quitting monastic life. What teaching was he given?
title: The Story about the Novice Saṅkicca
synopsis: CST4 & PTS Saṁkiccasāmaṇeravatthu Elder Sāriputta’s nephew Saṅkicca ordained as a novice, and when thirty bhikkhus’ lives were threatened by five hundred thieves he converted the thieves and they ordained; when he heard about it, this is the teaching the Buddha gave.
verse_english: Dhp 110: Better to live a single day ethical and absorbed in meditation than to live a hundred years unethical and lacking immersion.

question: Someone punched a senior monk in the back to see if he would get angry. What was taught about that?
title: The Story about the Elder Sāriputta
synopsis: A Brahmin thought Elder Sāriputta didn’t get angry because he had never been tested, so he walked up behind him and landed a great blow on his back; Elder Sāriputta was unperturbed, the Brahmin asked forgiveness and asked him to accept a meal, which he did; the Buddha commented on the incident in some verses.
verse_english: Dhp 389: One should never strike a brahmin, nor should a brahmin retaliate. Woe to the one who hurts a brahmin, and woe for the one who retaliates. / Dhp 390: Nothing is better for a brahmin than to hold their mind back from attachment. From wherever a cruel wish recoils, right there suffering subsides.

question: Someone punched a senior monk in the back to see if he would get angry. What was taught about that?
title: The Story about the Group of Six
synopsis: The Group of Six bhikkhus, whose unrestrained behaviour was the occasion for the Buddha laying down many of the Vinaya Regulations, put on clogs and clattered around on a rock; the Buddha advised them with some verses.
verse_english: Dhp 231: Guard against ill-tempered deeds, be restrained in body. Giving up bad bodily conduct, conduct yourself well in body. / Dhp 232: Guard against ill-tempered words, be restrained in speech. Giving up bad verbal conduct, conduct yourself well in speech. / Dhp 233: Guard against ill-tempered thoughts, be restrained in mind. Giving up bad mental conduct, conduct yourself well in mind. / Dhp 234: An attentive one is restrained in body restrained also in speech, in thought, too, they are restrained: they are restrained in every way.

question: Someone punched a senior monk in the back to see if he would get angry. What was taught about that?
title: The Story about the Pig Peta
synopsis: Elder Moggallāna saw a Peta with a pig’s head and reported it to the Buddha who explained that in a previous life he was someone who broke up a sincere friendship, and after arising in Avīci, the hell of relentless suffering, was later reborn as a Peta with a pig’s head because of his misdeed, and then the Buddha spoke a verse. Elder Mahā Moggallāna, Elder Lakkhaṇa, Buddha Kassapa,
verse_english: Dhp 281: Guarded in speech, restrained in mind, doing no unskillful bodily deed. Purify these three ways of performing deeds, and win the path known to seers.

question: Someone punched a senior monk in the back to see if he would get angry. What was taught about that?
title: The Story about a Certain Bhikkhu
synopsis: A bhikkhu was given a subject of meditation, went to the forest, and became an Arahat; as he was travelling a woman who had quarrelled with her husband followed close behind; when the husband saw them he thrashed the bhikkhu; the bhikkhus could not believe he had not got angry with the man, but the Buddha confirmed his purity with a verse.
verse_english: Dhp 405: They’ve laid aside violence against creatures firm and frail; not killing or making others kill: that’s who I declare a brahmin.

question: Someone punched a senior monk in the back to see if he would get angry. What was taught about that?
title: The Story about the Elder Sāriputta
synopsis: Elder Sāriputta would always bow in the direction where he knew his first Dhamma teacher Elder Assaji was living; the bhikkhus thought he was worshipping the cardinal points and reported the matter to the Buddha who explained the situation, and then taught them with a verse.
verse_english: Dhp 392: You should graciously honor the one from whom you learn the Dhamma taught by the awakened Buddha, as a brahmin honors the sacred flame.

question: Someone punched a senior monk in the back to see if he would get angry. What was taught about that?
title: The Story about the Group of Six
synopsis: The Group of Six bhikkhus fought with and chased off the Group of Seventeen bhikkhus, and took their rooms; the Buddha laid down a rule against violence and spoke a verse.
verse_english: Dhp 129: All tremble at the rod, all fear death. Treating others like oneself, neither kill nor incite to kill.

question: Someone punched a senior monk in the back to see if he would get angry. What was taught about that?
title: The Story about a Certain Bhikkhu
synopsis: Against the pleas of a Devatā a bhikkhu cut down a tree thereby injuring her child at the same time; the Devatā at first thought to kill him, but restrained her anger and reported the matter to the Buddha instead, who spoke a verse and gave her a new tree to live in, and laid down a rule that bhikkhus should not injure trees and plants.
verse_english: Dhp 222: When anger surges like a lurching chariot, keep it in check. That’s what I call a charioteer; others just hold the reins.

question: Someone punched a senior monk in the back to see if he would get angry. What was taught about that?
title: The Story about the Elder Suvaṇṇakāra
synopsis: Elder Sāriputta’s young disciple made no progress with his meditation subject so he took him to the Buddha, who, understanding his inclinations, gave him a different subject: to look upon a lotus flower, which soon disintegrated, giving the young bhikkhu insight into impermanence; the Buddha then appeared and gave this instruction.
verse_english: Dhp 285: Cut out affection for oneself, like plucking an autumn lotus. Foster only the path to peace, the extinguishment the Holy One taught.

question: A monk picked up a cloth he thought had been thrown away and handed it back when the owner turned up. Was that stealing?
title: The Story about a Treacherous Bhikkhu
synopsis: One bhikkhu of Devadatta’s faction persuaded another bhikkhu to share in the rich offerings they were receiving; even though he disagreed with Devadatta he joined them for the food; later when he returned to the Buddha he was reproved for not being content, and the Buddha taught the bhikkhus with some verses.
verse_english: Dhp 365: A well-off mendicant ought not look down on others, nor should they be envious. A mendicant who envies others does not achieve immersion. / Dhp 366: If a mendicant is poor in offerings, the well-to-do ought not look down on them. For the gods indeed praise them, who are tireless and pure of livelihood.

question: A monk picked up a cloth he thought had been thrown away and handed it back when the owner turned up. Was that stealing?
title: The Story about the Lay Disciple Mahā Kāla
synopsis: The householder Mahā Kāla listened to an all-night Dhamma teaching at Jetavana, but in the morning was beaten to death by people who mistook him for a thief; the Buddha explained that he had caused the unjust death of another in a previous life, and his bad deed had caught up with him, and gave a teaching in a verse.
verse_english: Dhp 161: For the evil that is done by oneself, born and produced in oneself, grinds down a simpleton, as diamond grinds a lesser gem.

question: A monk picked up a cloth he thought had been thrown away and handed it back when the owner turned up. Was that stealing?
title: The Story about a Certain Elder
synopsis: A certain bhikkhu picked up a cloth one day thinking it was discarded, only to be accosted by its owner to whom he straightaway gave the cloth back; when the bhikkhus heard about it they teased him and reported it to the Buddha who confirmed he did not take what was not given as he was without attachments, and then spoke a verse about him.
verse_english: Dhp 409: They don’t steal anything in the world, long or short, tiny or huge, beautiful or ugly: that’s who I declare a brahmin.

question: A monk picked up a cloth he thought had been thrown away and handed it back when the owner turned up. Was that stealing?
title: The Story about a Certain Bhikkhu
synopsis: A bhikkhu was given a meditation subject but could make no progress, so he determined to return to the Buddha; on his way he saw a great fire burn down a forest, and the Buddha appeared to him and taught him with a verse.
verse_english: Dhp 31: A mendicant who loves diligence, seeing fear in negligence— advances like fire, burning up fetters big and small.

question: A monk picked up a cloth he thought had been thrown away and handed it back when the owner turned up. Was that stealing?
title: The Story about the Elder Pilotika
synopsis: The poor man Pilotika was ordained by Elder Ānanda, grew fat and discontented, and thought to return to the lay life; but finding his previous rags he took them as a meditation subject and soon became an Arahat; the Buddha confirmed his status to the bhikkhus and spoke some verses.
verse_english: Dhp 143: Can a person constrained by conscience be found in the world? Who shies away from blame, like a fine horse from the whip? / Dhp 144: Like a fine horse under the whip, be keen and full of urgency. With faith, ethics, and energy, immersion, and investigation of principles, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, mindful, give up this vast suffering.

question: A monk picked up a cloth he thought had been thrown away and handed it back when the owner turned up. Was that stealing?
title: The Story about the Fruits and Powers of People’s Bad Conduct
synopsis: Elder Moggallāna saw a Peta dressed as a bhikkhu flying through the air with body all on fire and reported it to the Buddha, who told that previously the Peta had been a bhikkhu under Buddha Kassapa, but had not lived accordingly, and then he spoke a verse.
verse_english: Dhp 307: Many who wear a scrap of ocher cloth are unrestrained and wicked. Being wicked, they are reborn in hell due to their bad deeds.

question: A monk picked up a cloth he thought had been thrown away and handed it back when the owner turned up. Was that stealing?
title: The Story about the Elder Culla Panthaka
synopsis: When Elder Culla Panthaka could not remember even four lines of verse after three months trying, the Buddha asked him to rub a white cloth, which subsequently became soiled and gave him initial insight into impermanence; the Buddha then taught him that the mind is also defiled and must be cleansed, and he soon attained deliverance, after which the Buddha spoke a verse about him. Lives, Bodhisatta, Radiant Image, Previous Buddhas
verse_english: Dhp 25: By hard work and diligence, by restraint and by self-control, a smart person would build an island that the floods cannot overflow.
